info.name: Healthcare Treatment Journey — Service API
info.description:
Drives the inpatient admission-to-discharge journey through the healthcare-treatment-service REST API.

The service owns the Camunda credentials and talks to the cluster on your behalf, so nothing here needs an OAuth token or a cluster URL — only `baseUrl`.

## Setup

1. Import this collection and `healthcare-treatment-journey.postman_environment.json`.
2. Select the **Healthcare Treatment Journey — Local** environment.
3. Start the service (see the project README). Confirm with **00 Health → Service health**.

## Running

Folders 01 and 02 are ordered and work top to bottom in the Collection Runner.

Zeebe is eventually consistent — a task does not appear the instant the previous one completes. Every `Await …` request re-invokes itself via `setNextRequest` until the expected element shows up, capped by `pollCount`. **Set the Runner delay to 1000 ms** so polling does not spin.

## The vitals loop

Folder 01 drives the revise-plan loop for real: the patient breaches on the first observation, the discharge gate holds them back, the physician revises the plan, and the second observation clears them. No diversion is used to get through it.

That loop only converges because the vitals element folds both counters into `businessKey` (`caseId + "-vitals-" + directorReviewCount + "-" + dischargeAttemptCount`). The framework's `IdempotencyGuard` keys on `(businessKey, elementId)`, and both are otherwise identical on every pass — so without that mapping the second `vitals-monitoring` execution is misread as an at-least-once redelivery and completed without running, `vitalsTrend` stays `DETERIORATING`, and the journey loops forever. The review counter is the outer term because clinical director review resets `dischargeAttemptCount` to zero.

`01.13` and `01.18` assert the key of each pass, so losing that mapping fails the run loudly rather than hanging.

## AI steps

`Task_HistorySummary` and `Task_DischargeSummary` are AI Agent connector tasks and need an `OPENAI_API_TOKEN` connector secret in Camunda Console. Without it both raise an incident. Each has a boundary error that routes the journey past the AI step rather than stranding it.

exec: // Applies to every request: surface transport and server faults immediately rather than
// letting a later assertion fail for an unrelated reason.

request.description: Confirms the service is up and that both its outbound dependencies — PostgreSQL and the Camunda cluster — are reachable. Run this first; every other request depends on both.

exec: // A fresh business key each run keeps the archive's unique constraint on case_id happy.
console.log('Started ' + b.caseId + ' as instance ' + b.processInstanceKey + ' on definition v' + b.version);

request.description:
Starts the journey. Omit `caseId` and the service generates one.

Note `vitalsSeverity`: the triage table recognises only CRITICAL and MODERATE for chest pain. Any other value — including a typo — falls through to the catch-all rule and yields GENERAL_CARE / P3 rather than a cardiac pathway.

exec: pm.test('Timed out waiting for ' + want, () => pm.expect.fail('Gave up after 25 polls'));

request.description: Polls until the Registration task appears. Re-invokes itself rather than relying on a fixed delay, because the engine indexes asynchronously.
Completes a task by BPMN element id — the service resolves the engine key. The same route also accepts a numeric user task key if you already hold one; see 02.2 for that form.

exec: console.log('Diagnostics fanned out; waiting at ' + hit.name);
pm.test('Timed out waiting for ' + want, () => pm.expect.fail('Gave up after 30 polls'));

request.description: Triage runs, then the diagnostics sub-process fans out one branch per ordered test. The ECG branch is fully automated by LabTestOrderWorker and LabResultIngestionWorker; only the cardiology workup needs a human.

exec: // The ECG branch runs in parallel with the cardiology workup, so its order is not
// necessarily placed at the instant the human task appears - that independence is the
// point of the multi-instance stage. Poll for the order rather than assume it.
pm.test('Timed out waiting for the lab order', () => pm.expect.fail('orderId never appeared'));
console.log('Lab order raised by LabTestOrderWorker: ' + v.orderId);

request.description: Confirms the triage DMN fired and that the lab workers ran. `orderId` is proof that this service's own Java code executed — the engine handed it a job and LabTestOrderWorker answered.
Completing this closes the last open branch of the multi-instance diagnostics sub-process, so the join opens and the journey moves on to treatment planning.

exec: pm.test('Timed out waiting for ' + want, () => pm.expect.fail('Gave up after 30 polls'));

request.description: Waits for the diagnostics join to open and the treatment planning task to appear.
`consultsRequired: false` routes past the ad-hoc consultations sub-process. Set it true to exercise that branch instead.

exec: pm.test('Timed out waiting for ' + want, () => pm.expect.fail('Gave up after 30 polls'));

request.description: Waits for the treatment execution sub-process to open. The vitals-alert event sub-process lives inside this scope, so its message subscription is only active from here on.
Completing this triggers VitalsMonitorWorker, which breaches the thresholds on its first run, raises a VitalsAlert message into the event sub-process, and drives the discharge-readiness decision.

exec: // VitalsMonitorWorker runs asynchronously after the treatment step completes, so
// the trend is not there the instant this request fires.
pm.test('Vitals monitoring never ran', () => pm.expect.fail('vitalsTrend never appeared'));
// The vitals task scopes its idempotency key per loop pass, but that is a zeebe:input
// mapping, but the alert handler inside the event sub-process maps one too, and
// that one does surface here. It must NOT be the bare caseId: keyed that way the
// framework guard treats every alert after the first on a case as a replay and
// completes it silently, so a repeat breach is never handled. It is now derived
// from the monitoring pass that raised it - caseId-vitals-<review>-<attempt>-alert.
pm.test('alert key is scoped per alert, not per case', () => pm.expect(v.businessKey).to.eql(pm.environment.get('caseId') + '-vitals-0-0-alert'));
pm.test('alert key is not the bare caseId', () => pm.expect(v.businessKey).to.not.eql(pm.environment.get('caseId')));
console.log('Pass 1: trend=' + v.vitalsTrend + ' businessKey=' + v.businessKey + ' attempts=' + v.dischargeAttemptCount);
console.log('The discharge gate rejects, the counter increments, and the journey loops back to treatment planning.');

request.description: The patient breaches on the first observation, so the discharge gate holds them back and the journey loops round for a revised plan. That is the intended clinical path, not a fault.

exec: pm.test('loop returned to treatment planning', () => pm.expect(hit.elementId).to.eql(want));
console.log('Loop closed — the physician is asked to revise the plan.');
pm.test('Timed out waiting for ' + want, () => pm.expect.fail('Loop never came back round'));

request.description: The gate rejected, so the readiness task's own output mapping bumped `dischargeAttemptCount` and the discharge gateway routed back to treatment planning. Above three attempts the same gateway diverts to clinical director review instead.
The revised plan is what the patient responds to, which is what lets the loop terminate.

exec: pm.test('Timed out waiting for ' + want, () => pm.expect.fail('Gave up after 30 polls'));

request.description: Second entry into the treatment execution sub-process.
Triggers the second vitals check. This is the pass that used to be silently skipped.

exec: // Wait for the second vitals check to land. Its key is scoped to review 0 / attempt 1,
// a distinct execution rather than a replay of attempt 0.
pm.test('Second vitals check never ran', () => pm.expect.fail('businessKey stuck at ' + v.businessKey + ' — the guard is suppressing the loop pass'));
pm.test('second pass ran under its own idempotency key', () => pm.expect(v.businessKey).to.eql(secondPassKey));
console.log('Gate opened on its own — no diversion needed to reach discharge.');

request.description:
The heart of the regression.

The vitals element folds both counters into its idempotency key - caseId-vitals-<directorReviewCount>-<dischargeAttemptCount>. Without the attempt counter both passes key on (caseId, Task_VitalsMonitor), the second is misread as an at-least-once redelivery and completes without running, and vitalsTrend stays DETERIORATING forever. Without the review counter the same thing happens one step later: Task_ClinDirectorReview resets dischargeAttemptCount to 0, which regenerates the first pass's key, so the vitals check immediately after a senior clinician intervenes is silently skipped and the discharge gate decides on a stale trend.

businessKey visible here is the alert handler's, which is derived from the monitoring pass that raised the alert. 01.18 checks the vitals task's own key for the second pass.

exec: pm.test('Timed out waiting for ' + want, () => pm.expect.fail('Gave up after 30 polls'));

request.description: Waits for the diversion to take effect.
The last human step. RecordArchiveWorker then writes the case to PostgreSQL and the instance completes.

exec: pm.test('finished without an open incident', () => pm.expect(b.hasIncident).to.eql(false));
pm.test('Timed out waiting for completion', () => pm.expect.fail('Still ' + b.state + ' after 30 polls'));

request.description: Polls the instance until the engine reports COMPLETED.

exec: pm.test('Archive row never appeared', () => pm.expect.fail('RecordArchiveWorker did not write the case'));
// The archived trend is the clearest end-to-end signal that the loop converged:
// it is written by RecordArchiveWorker from the value the second vitals pass produced.
pm.test('archived trend reflects the recovered patient', () => pm.expect(r.vitalsTrend).to.be.oneOf(['IMPROVING', 'STABLE']));
console.log('Archived: ' + r.caseId + ' / ' + r.patientName + ' / ' + r.carePlan + ' / vitalsTrend=' + r.vitalsTrend);

request.description:
Reads the row RecordArchiveWorker wrote to PostgreSQL, straight through the service's own JPA adapter. This is the end-to-end proof: the engine ran the process, the service's Java code handled the archive job, and the data landed in the database.

`vitalsTrend` reads IMPROVING here. A DETERIORATING value would mean the second vitals pass never ran and the journey only reached discharge by intervention.
`diagnosticSystemDown: true` makes the diagnostics step throw the BPMN error DIAGNOSTIC_SYSTEM_UNAVAILABLE, which the boundary error event catches.

exec: body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ completedBy: 'registration-desk', variables: { consentObtained: true } }) }
pm.test('Timed out waiting for Registration', () => pm.expect.fail('Gave up after 25 polls'));

request.description: Polls for the task, then completes it by engine key from the test script — exercising the numeric-segment branch of `/cases/{key}/tasks/{idOrKey}/completion` alongside the element-id form used everywhere else.

exec: pm.test('boundary error routed to physician escalation', () => pm.expect(hit.elementId).to.eql(want));
pm.test('Timed out waiting for ' + want, () => pm.expect.fail('Escalation never appeared'));

request.description: The diagnostics sub-process throws DIAGNOSTIC_SYSTEM_UNAVAILABLE, the boundary error event catches it, and the journey diverts to physician escalation instead of continuing to treatment.

exec: console.log('Exception-path instance cancelled — it is parked on a human step by design.');

request.description: The escalation task has no automated follow-through, so the instance would sit there forever. Cancelling keeps the cluster tidy between runs.
Evaluates the decision table directly, without running a process — the fastest way to check a rule change.
The pathway the happy path takes.
Rule 3 ignores admission type — it matches on complaint and severity alone.
Rule 4 leaves severity blank, so any neurological complaint is P1 even when presenting mildly.

exec: console.warn('A chest-pain patient was routed to GENERAL_CARE / P3 / GENERAL ward because vitalsSeverity was SEVERE.');
console.warn('The table recognises only CRITICAL and MODERATE for chest pain; anything else hits the catch-all.');
console.warn('Nothing validates this input, so a typo silently downgrades a cardiac patient.');

request.description:
Documents a real gap rather than a feature. `SEVERE` reads like a valid severity but is not in the table's vocabulary, so a chest-pain patient drops from CARDIAC_CRITICAL / P1 / CCU to GENERAL_CARE / P3 / GENERAL.

The hit policy is FIRST and rule 5 matches anything, so the fall-through is silent. Worth either constraining the input to an enum or adding an explicit unmatched-severity rule.
Proves the decision table is not the reason the happy path stalls.

exec: console.log('STABLE clears too, so a patient who has held a clean state is not trapped in the loop.');

request.description: Together with 03.6, confirms both recovered trends open the gate. When the loop was stuck this pair proved the decision table was sound and the stale trend feeding it was at fault.
The verdict the first loop pass gets, which is what sends the journey back for a revised plan.
Where is this journey waiting right now?

Every process variable, JSON payloads parsed rather than returned as escaped strings.

Expect connector plumbing — `url`, `method`, `headers`, `body`, `authentication` — to appear at process scope after the AI task fails. Those are the connector's own inputs leaking into process scope because it raised an incident before scoping its outputs.
Includes resolved incidents, so a diverted AI task still shows here with state RESOLVED.

Useful when a diversion returns 409 — it tells you what is actually active, which is what `fromElementId` must name.

Results lag a second or two behind a modification; if the list looks stale, send it again.

exec: console.log('Published. 202 means the engine accepted the message, not that it correlated.');
console.log('The VitalsAlert subscription lives inside SubProcess_Treatment, so it only catches while the journey is inside treatment execution.');

request.description:
Correlates a VitalsAlert message by `caseId` into the non-interrupting event sub-process.

The subscription is scoped to SubProcess_Treatment, so publishing while the journey sits elsewhere — at Task_TreatmentPlan after a loop, for instance — succeeds but correlates nothing until the message TTL expires. Check for `alertSource` in the variables to confirm it landed.

exec: // In a full-collection run the happy-path instance has already completed by now,
// and the engine answers 404 for an instance that no longer exists. That is the
// correct outcome, not a failure — assert on either.
console.log('Instance already finished — nothing to cancel.');

request.description:
Terminates the journey. Use it to clear an instance left parked on a human step.

Returns 404 if the instance has already finished — which is what happens when the whole collection is run in order, since the happy path completes its instance.
